# What Is EDI? A Plain-English Guide for Shopify Stores

Chris I

October 30, 2026

**EDI (electronic data interchange) is a set of standard business documents that lets your store and your suppliers exchange inventory levels, purchase orders, shipping notices and invoices automatically, with no one retyping anything.** For a Shopify store that sells products it does not stock itself, EDI is what keeps the storefront honest: products show as available only when a supplier can ship them, orders reach the right supplier automatically, and tracking numbers flow back to customers on their own.

This guide explains what EDI is in plain terms, which documents matter for an online store, how an order moves from checkout to delivery, how the files travel, and how to tell whether your store needs it yet. It draws on the supplier connections we built for [Spooky Costumes](https://www.nativecode.ai/spooky-costumes-case-study) and [ThirdLust](https://www.nativecode.ai/thirdlust-case-study), two Shopify stores with catalogs of more than 8,000 and 11,000 products.

## What is EDI?

EDI is a shared language for business documents. Instead of a supplier emailing a PDF invoice or a spreadsheet of stock levels, both sides send structured files in an agreed format that software can read without a person in the loop.

In North America the dominant format is [X12](https://ecommerce.x12.org/industry/supply-chain), a standard chartered by ANSI and maintained for more than 40 years. X12 defines "transaction sets", each one a document type with a three-digit number. The 850 is a purchase order, the 856 is a ship notice, and so on. Outside North America the equivalent standard is EDIFACT, which uses names instead of numbers but does the same job.

The key idea is that each document has a fixed structure. A purchase order always carries the same kinds of fields in the same places: who is buying, what, how many, at what price and where to ship it. That predictability is what lets a store and a supplier automate the whole order cycle, even when they run completely different systems.

## Why would a Shopify store need EDI?

Most stores never need EDI. Three business models almost always do.

- **Dropship and large supplier catalogs.** If several suppliers hold your stock and ship directly to customers, every order has to reach the right supplier, and every stock change has to reach your store. Doing that by email and spreadsheet gets harder to keep accurate as the catalog grows.
- **Selling to big retailers.** Large retailers and marketplaces trade with suppliers over EDI. If you want to sell through them, you will be asked to send and receive their documents.
- **Buying from established distributors.** Many wholesale and distribution businesses only take orders over EDI, or charge for manual ones.

Spooky Costumes is an example of the first model. Its catalog runs to more than 8,000 products, and we built EDI connections to its suppliers for inventory and order routing, so stock levels and orders move between the store and each supplier without manual entry.

## The documents that move an online order

X12 lists more than 50 transaction sets used in the supply chain, but an online store typically needs only six. The table shows each one, who sends it, and what it does for the store.

| Document | Sent by | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 846 Inventory Inquiry/Advice | Supplier | Reports how many units of each item the supplier can ship. Your store uses it to update available quantities. |
| 850 Purchase Order | Store | Tells the supplier what to ship, to whom, at what cost. One customer order can become several POs if items sit with different suppliers. |
| 855 Purchase Order Acknowledgment | Supplier | Confirms the supplier accepted the order, or flags items it cannot fill. |
| 856 Ship Notice/Manifest | Supplier | Says what shipped, in which package, with which carrier and tracking number. Often called the ASN. |
| 810 Invoice | Supplier | Bills the store for what shipped, so costs can be matched to orders. |
| 997 Functional Acknowledgment | Both | A receipt that confirms a document arrived and could be read. It does not mean the order was accepted. |

Marketplaces with dropship programs use the same set. Amazon's Direct Fulfillment program, for example, is listed with the [846, 850, 855, 856 and 810](https://www.stacksync.com/edi/amazon/amazon-dropship-direct-fulfillment/x12-846-inventory-inquiry-advice). Each trading partner publishes its own implementation guide, which says which version, fields and rules it expects, so the same document number can still need different mapping for each supplier.

## How an order flows from checkout to delivery

Here is the full cycle for one dropship order, with the document that carries each step.

1. **Stock arrives.** Each supplier sends an 846 on an agreed schedule. Your store updates the available quantity for every mapped SKU, so products sell out when the supplier sells out.
2. **A customer checks out.** The order lands in Shopify as usual.
3. **The order is split and routed.** The integration groups the order lines by supplier and sends each supplier an 850 for its share, with the customer's shipping address.
4. **The supplier confirms.** A 997 comes back to say the file arrived. An 855 follows to accept the order or to reject or backorder specific lines.
5. **The supplier ships.** An 856 arrives with carrier and tracking details. The integration creates a fulfillment in Shopify, which sends the customer their shipping email.
6. **The supplier bills.** An 810 arrives. The integration matches it to the purchase order and the shipment, so finance only reviews the mismatches.

When this runs well, nobody on your team touches a routine order. People only step in when something does not match: a rejected line, a late shipment, an invoice for the wrong quantity.

## How the files travel: AS2, VAN, SFTP or a provider

The documents are the language. The transport is how they get from one system to the other. Walmart's supplier documentation describes the [four common options](https://developer.walmart.com/suppliers/docs/edi-connection-types) well, and most trading partners offer some mix of them.

| Connection | How it works | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AS2 | A direct, point-to-point connection. Files are encrypted and signed with digital certificates, and each side gets a delivery receipt. | High-volume partners who want a direct, secure link |
| VAN (value-added network) | A third-party network that acts as a mailbox between partners and passes documents along. | Partners who already route everything through a VAN |
| SFTP | Both sides drop and collect files on a secure server. | Smaller suppliers and simpler setups |
| Solution provider | An EDI platform handles the connection and translation for you, and exchanges data with your store through an API. | Stores that want one connection point for many suppliers |

You rarely get to pick freely. Large partners often require a specific method, and your setup has to support whatever each supplier uses.

## EDI, APIs and CSV feeds: which one when

EDI is not the only way to connect a store to a supplier. Many smaller suppliers offer a CSV inventory file or a modern API instead, and that is fine. What matters is that every supplier's data ends up in the same shape inside your store.

| Method | Strengths | Weaknesses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| X12 EDI | Standard documents, required by large retailers and distributors, built for high volume | Each partner has its own rules, setup takes testing, needs translation for Shopify |
| Supplier API | Real-time, flexible, easy to read | Every supplier's API is different, so each one is its own build |
| CSV or spreadsheet feed | Easy for any supplier to produce | No standard layout, easy to break, usually only covers inventory |

In practice, most stores with many suppliers end up with a mix. Whatever the mix, the goal is the same: every supplier's data is translated into the same inventory, order and fulfillment updates in the store.

## Where Shopify fits

Shopify does not read or write X12 documents itself. It works through its Admin API, which handles inventory levels, orders and fulfillments. An EDI integration sits between the two and translates in both directions.

- An incoming 846 becomes inventory level updates on the matching Shopify variants.
- A new Shopify order becomes one 850 per supplier.
- An incoming 856 becomes a fulfillment with carrier and tracking number attached.
- An incoming 810 is matched against the order and shipment records for reconciliation.

That layer can be an EDI app, a third-party EDI platform, or a custom integration. The right choice depends on how many suppliers you have, which connection methods they require, and how much control you need over routing rules. The constant across all of them is SKU mapping: every supplier item number has to map cleanly to a product variant in your store, or nothing else works.

## What usually goes wrong

EDI fails quietly. A document that does not process rarely causes an error a customer sees right away. It shows up later as an oversell, a missing tracking number or a billing dispute. These are the problems we check for first.

- **SKU mismatches.** A supplier renames or retires an item number and its stock stops updating. The product keeps selling on a quantity that is no longer true.
- **Old data overwriting new data.** If an older inventory file is processed after a newer one, stock goes backwards. Each update needs a timestamp check.
- **On-hand versus available.** Suppliers report different quantity types. Selling against on-hand stock that is already reserved for other retailers causes oversells.
- **Partial shipments and backorders.** One order can ship in several packages, or have lines that never ship. The integration has to handle each case and tell the customer correctly.
- **Cancellations.** A customer cancels after the purchase order went out. Each supplier handles cancellation differently, and some need a phone call.
- **Silent failures.** A 997 says a file arrived, not that the order is fine. Without monitoring for missing 855s and late 856s, problems sit unnoticed for days.

## How do you know if your store needs EDI?

You probably need EDI, or at least an automated supplier integration, if two or more of these are true.

- More than one supplier ships directly to your customers.
- Your catalog has thousands of SKUs that you do not physically stock.
- Someone on your team updates inventory or forwards orders by hand every day.
- You have sold items a supplier could not ship.
- Customers ask where their order is because tracking was never entered.
- A retailer, marketplace or distributor has asked you to trade over EDI.

If only one is true, a simpler feed or app may be enough for now. The aim is not to adopt EDI for its own sake. It is to stop selling stock you do not have and stop paying people to move data between systems.

## How we build supplier connections

Our [EDI and ecommerce operations](https://www.nativecode.ai/services/edi-integration) work follows four steps, and we go live one supplier at a time.

1. **Map.** Document every supplier, the formats and connection methods they accept, their implementation guides, and how orders move today.
2. **Connect.** Build the EDI, API or feed connection for each supplier and map its item numbers and fields to your store.
3. **Test.** Run test orders end to end with each supplier, including rejections, partial shipments and cancellations, before live orders flow.
4. **Run.** Go live supplier by supplier, with monitoring for failed documents, stock mismatches and late shipments, and a clear owner for each exception.

Because supplier data also drives product titles, attributes and collections, we tie the integration to the store's [Shopify architecture](https://www.nativecode.ai/services/shopify-seo), so new supplier products arrive ready to rank as well as ready to sell.

## Frequently asked questions

### What does EDI stand for?

EDI stands for electronic data interchange. It is the exchange of standard business documents, such as purchase orders, inventory updates, ship notices and invoices, between two company systems without anyone retyping them. Most US retail and ecommerce EDI uses the X12 standard, where each document has a number, such as the 850 purchase order or the 846 inventory update.

### Does Shopify support EDI?

Shopify does not process EDI documents natively. Stores connect to suppliers through an EDI app, a third-party EDI platform or a custom integration. The integration translates incoming EDI documents into Shopify inventory, order and fulfillment updates through the Shopify Admin API, and turns Shopify orders into purchase orders the supplier system can read.

### What is the difference between an 855 and a 997?

A 997 Functional Acknowledgment only confirms that a document arrived and could be read. An 855 Purchase Order Acknowledgment confirms whether the supplier accepted the order, and can reject or backorder individual lines. A store needs both to know an order is really on its way.

### Is EDI the same as an API?

No. EDI uses standard document formats, such as X12, that many companies share, usually sent as files in batches. An API is a direct software connection defined by one company, usually in real time. Many stores use both, depending on what each supplier offers.

## Where to start

List every supplier that ships to your customers, how each one sends you stock levels today, and how orders reach them. That one page usually shows exactly where orders and inventory are being moved by hand, and which suppliers to connect first.

If you want help mapping it, [talk to us](https://www.nativecode.ai/company/contact). We will review your suppliers and order flow and tell you plainly whether you need EDI, a simpler feed, or nothing yet.

# Why Most Websites Stop Growing After Year One

Chris I

February 2, 2026

Most websites stop growing after year one because their structure does not scale with their content. As pages pile up, internal links thin out, topics overlap and compete, and crawlers spend time on the wrong URLs. Publishing more rarely fixes it. Restructuring taxonomy, internal linking and topic clusters usually does.

Launching a new website represents a defining milestone for brands, startups, and enterprise organizations. Teams invest heavily in design, content development, technical infrastructure, and marketing campaigns to establish early visibility and credibility. During the first year after launch, many websites experience encouraging organic growth. Traffic begins to increase, search rankings improve across multiple keyword clusters, and newly published content often gains traction in search results relatively quickly.

However, by the second year, growth frequently slows or becomes unpredictable. Organic traffic may plateau, new content struggles to rank competitively, and pages that previously performed well can begin to lose visibility. Organizations often respond by publishing more content, increasing promotional efforts, or expanding paid acquisition strategies. While these tactics may produce temporary improvements, they rarely address the underlying causes of growth stagnation.

The reality is that organic slowdowns rarely occur because teams run out of ideas or marketing creativity. More commonly, websites reach structural limitations. As content libraries expand, internal linking systems weaken, topical authority becomes fragmented, and search engines struggle to interpret relationships between pages. Without intentional structural planning, growth naturally slows regardless of publishing volume.

At NativeCode, we consistently observe that sustainable organic growth depends far more on architecture and content relationships than on content production alone. Websites that invest in scalable structural SEO systems often unlock entirely new growth opportunities, even when content output remains steady.

## Why does early organic growth happen naturally?

Most websites experience their strongest organic momentum during their first twelve months. Several structural advantages exist during early development phases that make ranking growth easier to achieve.

### Limited Internal Competition Strengthens Ranking Signals

During early development, websites typically contain fewer pages targeting overlapping search queries. When new content is published, search engines can easily determine which page best satisfies user intent. Without internal competition between multiple similar pages, ranking signals such as backlinks, engagement metrics, and relevance indicators consolidate around individual assets rather than becoming diluted across competing content.

This clarity allows early blog articles, landing pages, and educational resources to gain traction quickly. As a result, many organizations assume that publishing frequency alone drives organic growth, when in reality structural simplicity is playing a significant role.

### Crawl Efficiency Is Higher on Smaller Websites

Search engines allocate crawl resources based on domain authority, site complexity, and perceived content value. Smaller websites benefit from streamlined navigation structures, limited URL variations, and reduced duplicate content risks. These advantages allow search crawlers to easily discover, interpret, and index new pages.

Efficient crawling enables faster ranking improvements and accelerates early growth momentum. As websites expand, maintaining crawl efficiency becomes significantly more challenging without structural optimization.

### Topical Authority Builds Faster With Concentrated Content Focus

New websites often concentrate content production around a limited number of core themes or service areas. This focused content strategy helps search engines associate the domain with specific expertise areas. When multiple early articles reinforce related topics, authority consolidates naturally and strengthens search relevance signals.

As content expands into additional verticals, product categories, or informational topics, maintaining concentrated topical authority becomes increasingly difficult without intentional architecture planning.

## Why do growth challenges begin as websites scale?

Website expansion introduces structural complexity. Additional content creates overlapping topics, deeper navigation hierarchies, and more complicated internal linking relationships. Without governance frameworks, these changes gradually weaken organic performance.

### Authority Fragmentation Becomes a Major Risk

Rapid content expansion frequently results in multiple pages targeting similar search themes. Instead of strengthening overall topic coverage, authority signals become distributed across competing assets.

Search engines may struggle to determine which page represents the most authoritative answer for a given query. This uncertainty can lead to ranking volatility and prevent pages from achieving long-term stability. Authority fragmentation is one of the most common drivers of stalled organic growth, particularly for content-heavy websites and ecommerce ecosystems.

### Internal Linking Systems Gradually Break Down

Internal linking is often managed manually during early publishing stages. As content libraries expand, maintaining consistent linking strategies becomes increasingly difficult. New content frequently lacks connections to established authority pages, limiting its ability to inherit ranking strength.

Weak internal linking also disrupts crawl pathways, making it more difficult for search engines to interpret relationships between content assets across the site.

### Crawl Inefficiencies Increase With Scale

Large websites often introduce navigation filters, parameterized URLs, faceted search structures, and duplicate content pathways. These elements create excessive crawl demand, forcing search engines to allocate resources inefficiently.

When crawlers spend time indexing low-value or duplicate pages, high-priority content may remain undiscovered or experience delayed ranking improvements.

### Content Overlap Creates Internal Ranking Competition

Without structured search intent governance, websites frequently publish multiple pages covering similar keyword clusters. Instead of expanding search visibility, overlapping content creates internal ranking competition and reduces authority consolidation.

Content overlap confuses search engines and weakens the site’s ability to dominate specific topic areas.

## Why does publishing more content rarely solve growth plateaus?

When organic performance slows, many organizations increase content production volume. While fresh content remains important, publishing frequency alone cannot resolve structural SEO weaknesses.

### Search Engines Evaluate Content Ecosystems, Not Individual Pages

Modern search algorithms analyze how content assets relate to each other rather than ranking pages in isolation. Content that exists without strong internal relationships struggles to build sustained authority.

### AI-Driven Discovery Rewards Structured Knowledge Systems

AI-powered search platforms prioritize websites that demonstrate comprehensive subject expertise through interconnected content ecosystems. Websites lacking structured relationships between articles, category pages, and service content struggle to appear in conversational search results and AI-generated recommendations.

### Excess Publishing Can Create Structural Noise

Publishing aggressively without architecture planning frequently produces duplicate content clusters and overlapping topic coverage. Instead of expanding visibility, this approach increases internal competition and weakens authority signals across the domain.

## Hidden Structural Bottlenecks That Limit Growth

Many structural limitations develop gradually and remain unnoticed until organic growth slows significantly.

### Taxonomy Frameworks Often Fail to Scale

Category structures designed during early website development frequently lack long-term scalability. Weak parent-child relationships between categories, subcategories, and content assets reduce search clarity and limit authority distribution.

### Orphaned Pages Become Increasingly Common

As content libraries expand, pages often become disconnected from navigation systems or internal linking frameworks. Orphaned pages are difficult for search engines to discover and rarely achieve strong ranking performance.

### Content Clusters Lack Strategic Depth

Many websites publish multiple articles around similar topics but fail to establish clear cluster relationships. Without pillar content supported by structured subtopic articles, authority remains fragmented.

### Navigation Complexity Reduces Crawl Efficiency

As websites expand, navigation systems often become layered, inconsistent, or redundant. Complex navigation reduces crawl efficiency and creates friction for both users and search engines.

## Architecture Is the Foundation of Sustainable Organic Growth

Long-term SEO success depends heavily on scalable site architecture. Search engines rely on structured navigation and linking frameworks to interpret content relationships and authority signals.

### Pillar Content Creates Authority Anchors

Pillar pages provide comprehensive coverage of core topics. Supporting articles expand subtopics and reinforce content relationships within clusters. This structure improves ranking stability and helps search engines interpret topical depth.

### Entity Relationships Strengthen Search Relevance

Search engines increasingly evaluate websites through entity recognition and contextual relationships. Establishing clear relationships between categories, services, informational content, and brand expertise improves topical authority and contextual relevance.

### URL Hierarchies Improve Crawl Clarity

Logical URL structures reinforce content relationships and improve crawl efficiency. Structured taxonomy planning helps search engines understand how pages relate within the overall content ecosystem.

## Internal Linking Remains One of the Most Powerful SEO Growth Levers

Internal linking is frequently underestimated as a long-term SEO strategy, yet it plays a critical role in authority distribution and crawl optimization.

### Internal Links Distribute Authority Across Content Assets

Strategic linking allows ranking equity to flow from high-authority pages to supporting content. Structured linking ensures new articles benefit from established ranking signals.

### Crawl Pathways Improve Content Discovery Speed

Search engines rely heavily on internal links to discover new content. Strong linking frameworks improve crawl frequency and accelerate indexation.

### Contextual Linking Reinforces Topical Relationships

Links placed within relevant content strengthen relationships between related pages. This helps search engines interpret content depth and reinforces topical clusters.

### AI Search Is Redefining Organic Growth Models

AI-driven search platforms evaluate content through contextual understanding rather than keyword matching alone.

### Conversational Search Rewards Decision-Support Content

AI engines interpret queries as conversations rather than isolated keywords. Websites structured around topic ecosystems and decision-support content are more likely to appear in AI-generated answers.

### Entity Authority Is Replacing Keyword-Only Targeting

AI discovery platforms prioritize entity relationships and knowledge ecosystems. Websites built around entity-driven content clusters achieve stronger conversational search visibility.

### Content Completeness Influences AI Citation Visibility

AI platforms favor content that answers multiple related questions within unified topic clusters. Content lacking depth or relationship clarity struggles to appear in AI recommendations and citations.

## Measuring Growth Requires Structural Performance Metrics

Traffic growth alone does not accurately reflect SEO health. Sustainable growth requires evaluating how effectively content architecture supports discovery and authority consolidation.

Key structural performance indicators include:

• Crawl frequency and indexation efficiency
• Ranking stability across topic clusters
• Expansion of keyword cluster coverage
• Internal linking distribution strength
• AI citation and conversational search visibility

## Breaking Organic Growth Plateaus Requires Structural Optimization

Websites that successfully scale beyond early growth typically prioritize architecture optimization alongside content publishing.

### Content Relationship Audits Reveal Authority Gaps

Regular audits identify overlapping topics, orphaned pages, and cluster gaps that weaken authority signals and crawl efficiency.

### Internal Linking Systems Must Evolve With Content Expansion

Structured linking frameworks improve crawl efficiency and strengthen authority distribution across topic ecosystems.

### Taxonomy Hierarchies Should Be Continuously Refined

Clear parent-child relationships improve crawl clarity and strengthen topical authority signals.

### Content Depth Often Outperforms Topic Expansion

Expanding existing topic clusters frequently produces stronger growth results than launching unrelated subject areas.

## The Future of Organic Growth Will Be Architecture-Driven

As websites scale and AI discovery reshapes search behavior, architecture will become the primary differentiator between brands that achieve scalable growth and those that plateau.

Search visibility increasingly depends on how effectively websites structure content ecosystems, reinforce entity relationships, and maintain crawl efficiency. Publishing frequency alone will no longer determine organic success.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why does website traffic plateau after the first year?

Website traffic usually plateaus after the first year because the site structure stops keeping up with its content. As pages are added, internal links thin out, topics overlap and compete, and crawlers spend time on low-value URLs. Authority spreads across too many weak pages instead of building on a few strong ones.

### Will publishing more content fix an SEO plateau?

Usually not. Publishing more content into a weak structure tends to add overlap and noise rather than growth. Search engines and AI systems evaluate how content fits together, so restructuring taxonomy, consolidating overlapping pages and strengthening internal links usually does more than raising publishing volume.

### How does internal linking help SEO growth?

Internal linking distributes authority across your pages, helps crawlers find new content faster and shows search engines how topics relate. Contextual links from strong pages to related ones reinforce topic clusters. As a site grows, internal linking has to be maintained on purpose, or new pages end up orphaned and underperform.

### What is an orphaned page?

An orphaned page is a page with no internal links pointing to it. Search engines and visitors can only reach it through the sitemap, a direct link or an outside source, so it is crawled less often and gains little authority. Orphaned pages become common as sites grow without a clear taxonomy and linking plan.

## How NativeCode Supports Scalable Organic Growth

NativeCode specializes in architecture-led growth systems that align technical SEO, AI discovery optimization, and scalable content ecosystems. Our methodology strengthens taxonomy frameworks, rebuilds internal linking infrastructure, and designs entity-driven content relationships that support long-term discoverability.

Brands experiencing organic growth plateaus partner with NativeCode to restructure content ecosystems, eliminate structural bottlenecks, and unlock scalable acquisition opportunities across both traditional search engines and AI-driven discovery platforms.

# Why Your FAQ Isn't Getting Quoted by AI

Source: https://www.nativecode.ai/post/why-your-faq-isnt-getting-quoted (updated 2026-11-02)

[← All insights](https://www.nativecode.ai/blog)

[

AI Search & AEO

](https://www.nativecode.ai/blog-categories/ai-search-aeo)

# Why Your FAQ Isn't Getting Quoted

Chris I

August 31, 2026

**An FAQ block fails to get quoted when its answers cannot stand alone, which is usually because they were written for someone who has already read the page.** FAQ sections are the most citation-ready format on the web and the most consistently wasted, because the format is copied without the constraints that make it work.

Below are the six patterns that account for nearly all of it, each with a before-and-after and a test.

## Pattern 1: The answer starts with "Yes" or "No" and nothing else

A one-word opening carries no information once the passage is separated from its question. An extraction system may take the answer without the heading, and "Yes, absolutely, and it's easier than most people think" is a chunk that says nothing.

**Before:** *Q: Does AEO replace traditional SEO?*
*A: No, not at all. They work together.*

**After:** *A: AEO does not replace traditional SEO. The retrieval gates run in order, and crawlability and parsing are conventional technical SEO work that must succeed before extraction is possible.*

Answer with the polarity *and* the restated subject. "No" followed by the full proposition costs you eight words and makes the passage self-sufficient.

## Pattern 2: The question is not one anyone asks

FAQ questions written backwards from a keyword rather than forwards from a user produce phrasing no human types. "What are the benefits of AEO services for enterprise organisations?" is a heading, not a question.

The test: read the question aloud. If you would not say it to a colleague, a user did not type it into a prompt box.

Source real questions from sales call recordings, support tickets, the "People also ask" box, and the follow-up questions your own AI assistants suggest. Those are phrasings that exist in the wild and therefore have embeddings close to real queries.

## Pattern 3: The answer depends on the page around it

The most common failure, and the hardest to see when you are the author. An answer that says "as covered above," "this framework," or "the third option" is unusable once lifted.

**Before:** *A: It depends on which of the three approaches you chose earlier. The second one generally works better for larger catalogs.*

**After:** *A: For catalogs above roughly 10,000 SKUs, indexing only filter combinations with demonstrated search demand outperforms indexing all of them, because it concentrates crawl budget on pages that can rank.*

The rewrite names the threshold, the choice, and the reason. Nothing outside the paragraph is required to understand it.

## Pattern 4: The answer is too long to be an answer

An FAQ answer that runs 400 words is an article section wearing an FAQ's clothes. Extraction systems favour passages that resolve a question completely and briefly: roughly 40 to 120 words is the range that reads as an answer rather than a discussion.

If an answer genuinely needs more room, that is a signal it deserves its own section or its own article, with the FAQ carrying a short answer and a link to the longer treatment.

## Pattern 5: The FAQ exists only in schema

Some teams add `FAQPage` markup describing questions and answers that are not visible on the rendered page, on the theory that the markup is what machines read.

This is a contradiction between structured claims and rendered content, and it is the kind of mismatch a trust-weighted system is specifically built to catch. Google's structured data guidelines require FAQ content to be visible to users; markup describing invisible content is a violation, not a shortcut.

The correct order is always: write the visible FAQ, then mark up what is there.

## Pattern 6: Every answer ends in a pitch

An answer that resolves into "and that's exactly what our team helps with" trains extraction systems to treat the passage as promotional rather than informational. Promotional passages get retrieved less and cited less.

Keep the answer clean. Put the commercial move in a separate CTA block after the FAQ, where it belongs and where it does not contaminate a quotable passage.

## How do you test whether an FAQ answer can be quoted?

One procedure catches all six patterns. Copy a single answer, paste it into a blank document with no question above it, and read it.

Three questions about what you see. Does it state its own subject, or does it assume one? Can you tell what claim is being made without the question? Would it be useful to someone who arrived at this paragraph and nothing else?

If any answer is no, the pair fails. This test takes about fifteen seconds per answer and finds more real problems than any tool.

## How should FAQPage markup match the visible FAQ?

Once the visible FAQ is right, the markup is mechanical. Each pair maps to one `Question` with one `acceptedAnswer`, and the text in the markup must match the text on the page.

```
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "FAQPage",
  "mainEntity": [{
    "@type": "Question",
    "name": "Does AEO replace traditional SEO?",
    "acceptedAnswer": {
      "@type": "Answer",
      "text": "AEO does not replace traditional SEO. The retrieval gates run in order, and crawlability and parsing are conventional technical SEO work that must succeed before extraction is possible."
    }
  }]
}
```

Two rules worth holding to. Mark up only questions genuinely visible on the page. And keep the `text` value identical to the rendered answer, paraphrasing between markup and page reintroduces the mismatch problem the markup was meant to solve.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many questions should an FAQ section have?

Between four and eight questions suits a typical article. Beyond that, questions tend to become padding, and a page with thirty marginal questions dilutes the strong ones instead of adding coverage. Pick the questions buyers actually ask, answer each one completely and briefly, and cut the rest.

### Can FAQ schema alone get my page into AI answers?

No. Schema describes structure that already exists on the page. It cannot make an answer quotable if the visible text is not. A visible, self-contained FAQ with no markup will outperform markup that describes questions nobody can see, so write the visible FAQ first and mark up only what is there.

### Should FAQ answers repeat information from the article body?

Yes, some repetition is correct. An answer engine retrieves each chunk independently of the page it came from, so an FAQ answer that assumes the reader saw the body will not stand alone. Restating a definition or the key fact briefly is a feature of a good answer, not redundancy.

### Does it matter where the FAQ sits on the page?

Placement matters less than self-containment. Near the end of the article is conventional and works well, because it lets the body carry the argument and the FAQ carry short answers that can be lifted on their own. What matters most is that every answer makes sense without the page around it.

## Where to start

Take the FAQ on your highest-value page and run the extraction test on every answer. In most cases a majority fail on pattern 3, and the fix is a single rewritten opening sentence per answer, perhaps twenty minutes of work for the whole block.

# Wikidata and Entity Grounding for AI Search

# Wikipedia, Wikidata, and Entity Grounding

Chris I

August 31, 2026

**Entity grounding is the process by which an AI system resolves who you are before it evaluates anything you published.** A model that cannot confidently identify your organisation has no reason to name it in an answer, regardless of how well your pages are structured. This is the GEO layer, brand-level rather than page-level, and it sits underneath everything AEO does.

The strongest grounding signals come from sources you do not control. That is the whole point of them, and it is why this work is slower and more valuable than on-page optimisation.

## What are the four corroboration layers?

Think of every claim about your company as sitting on one of four levels, ordered by how much independent verification it carries.

**Layer 1: owned prose.** Your about page, your homepage copy. Self-made and unverified. A model can read it but has no basis to trust it over any competing description.

**Layer 2: owned structured data.** `Organization` schema with a `sameAs` array. Still self-made, but machine-readable and, crucially, pointing outward at sources that can be checked.

**Layer 3: third-party unstructured.** Press coverage, conference listings, podcast appearances, directory profiles, LinkedIn and Crunchbase entries. Independent, and the volume and consistency of these is what most brands are actually competing on.

**Layer 4: structured graph.** Wikidata and Wikipedia. Independent *and* machine-readable, which is why they carry disproportionate weight.

The practical objective of entity work is to move facts leftward, from claims only you make into sources that confirm them.

## Wikidata is the accessible one

Wikidata is a structured, openly editable knowledge base with a far lower inclusion bar than Wikipedia. It does not require the same notability threshold, and its items are explicitly designed for machine consumption.

A Wikidata item is a set of statements: instance of (business), industry, founder, headquarters location, inception date, official website, and identifiers linking to other databases. Each statement can carry a reference to a source.

Three things make it worth the effort. It is queryable via SPARQL, so systems can retrieve facts about you directly rather than inferring them from prose. Its identifiers act as a hub, connecting your entity across databases. And it is frequently used as a grounding source precisely because its structure removes ambiguity.

The rule that matters: **every statement should cite an independent source.** Unsourced statements are weak and may be removed. Do not create an item that merely restates your marketing copy.

## Wikipedia has a real notability bar, and most companies do not clear it

Wikipedia requires significant coverage in reliable, independent, secondary sources. Press releases do not count. Your own blog does not count. Routine funding announcements and directory listings generally do not count either.

Two failure modes are worth naming because both are common and both are damaging.

**Creating an article about your own company.** This is a conflict of interest under Wikipedia's guidelines. Articles created this way are frequently deleted, and the attempt is visible in public edit history.

**Paying for placement.** Undisclosed paid editing violates Wikipedia's terms of use. Beyond the ethics, it is detectable and the resulting article is usually removed, leaving a public record that is worse than having no article at all.

If you genuinely meet the notability bar, the correct route is to let an independent editor make that call, with a properly disclosed conflict-of-interest declaration if you are involved at all. If you do not meet it, the answer is to do things that generate genuine independent coverage, which is a business activity, not an SEO task.

## What should you do when Wikipedia is out of reach?

Most organisations are in this position, and it is not the constraint it appears to be. Layer 3 done thoroughly outperforms a thin layer 4 presence.

1. **Make your descriptions identical everywhere.** Your LinkedIn, Crunchbase, G2, industry directories, conference bios, and site should describe your company in consistent terms. Inconsistency is the single most common reason entity resolution fails: a system reading four different descriptions has four weak signals rather than one strong one.
2. **Populate `sameAs` with everything real.** Every profile you legitimately control belongs in that array. It is the bridge between your self-description and independent corroboration.
3. **Pursue coverage that would satisfy a Wikipedia editor.** Original research, genuine data, distinctive expertise: the things that earn independent write-ups. This builds layer 3 now and layer 4 eligibility later.
4. **Claim and complete every profile that exists.** Incomplete or outdated third-party profiles actively contradict your current positioning.

## How do you test your current entity grounding?

Two checks, both quick, neither requiring a tool.

**Ask the models directly.** Prompt several AI systems with "What is \[your company\]?" and compare. Confident, consistent, accurate answers mean grounding is working. Hedging, confusion with a similarly named company, or outdated descriptions tell you exactly which facts have not propagated.

**Search for your brand plus a disambiguator.** If your name collides with another entity, such as a common word or another company in a different sector, that collision is a grounding problem in its own right, and the fix is to strengthen the association between your name and your category everywhere it appears.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need a Wikipedia page for AI visibility?

No. A Wikipedia article is a strong grounding signal, but it requires significant independent coverage, and most companies do not qualify. Consistent third-party profiles and a well-referenced Wikidata item deliver much of the same benefit without the notability requirement, and they are within reach for most brands.

### Can I create my own Wikidata item?

Yes. Wikidata inclusion criteria are much broader than Wikipedia criteria, and self-creation is permitted, but every statement should cite an independent source. An item that only restates your own marketing carries little weight, so link it to press coverage, registries and other sources a model can check.

### Is it safe to pay someone to create a Wikipedia page?

No. Undisclosed paid editing breaches the Wikipedia terms of use, is often detected, and usually ends in deletion plus a permanent public record of the attempt. That outcome is worse than having no article. Earn independent coverage first and let editors with no stake in your company decide whether to write about you.

### What is the difference between GEO and AEO?

GEO works at the entity level: it makes an AI model understand who your brand is. AEO works at the page level: it makes a specific passage quotable. GEO decides whether you are a candidate for an answer at all, and AEO decides whether your page is the one that gets quoted. Most brands need both.

## Where to start

Ask three different AI systems what your company does and read the answers side by side. The inconsistencies are your grounding brief: each one points at a fact that exists only in your own copy and nowhere a model can verify it.

Fix the descriptions across your third-party profiles first, then populate `sameAs`. For entity strategy across a brand portfolio, that is a [strategy session](https://www.nativecode.ai/company/contact).

Related reading: our guide on [which schema types matter for AI citation](https://www.nativecode.ai/post/schema-markup-for-ai-citation), and how our [AI search optimization and AEO services](https://www.nativecode.ai/services/ai-seo) put this into practice.

# Digital marketing RFP template and agency scorecard.

This digital marketing RFP template gives you a Word brief with 27 questions for agencies and a weighted Excel scorecard, so you can brief agencies the same way and compare their answers on the same terms. NativeCode, an Atlanta-based digital marketing agency, built it. Edit it, send it, and score the proposals that come back.

01

A ready-to-send RFP in Word

Twelve sections from goals and scope to budget, timeline and submission rules, with guidance notes you delete before sending.

02

27 questions that separate agencies

Who does the work, the first 90 days, AI search measurement, data ownership and what happens if you part ways.

03

A weighted scorecard in Excel

Nine criteria, a 1 to 5 scoring guide, automatic totals and ranks, plus a 12-month pricing comparison.

Get the template

How to use it

## How do you run a fair agency search?

The template does the heavy lifting. These are the habits that make the difference between a confident decision and a beauty contest.

01

### Write a short brief

Goals with numbers, scope, budget range and timeline. Five clear pages beat a thirty-page questionnaire.

02

### Send it to three to five agencies

Enough to compare, few enough that each agency puts real effort into its answer.

03

### Score separately, then compare

Each reviewer fills in the scorecard alone before the group meets, so the loudest voice does not set the scores.

04

### Call the references

Ask who did the work, how problems were handled and whether they would hire the agency again.

FAQ

## Digital marketing RFP questions

### What should a digital marketing RFP include?

A digital marketing RFP should include a short company overview, the problem you want solved, goals with current and target numbers, the services in scope, your current tools and team, a budget range, a timeline, what each proposal must contain and how you will score it.

### How many agencies should receive the RFP?

Three to five agencies is enough for most companies. More than that adds review work without improving the decision, and agencies put less effort into crowded pitches. Send the same brief to each one, give them the same deadline and the same chance to ask questions, then score every proposal on the same scorecard.

### Should we share our budget in the RFP?

Yes, share it as a range. Without one, agencies guess at scope and you get proposals that cannot be compared side by side. A range does not commit you to spending the top of it, and it lets each agency show what it would prioritize at that level of investment.

### How long should the RFP process take?

Plan on four to eight weeks from sending the RFP to signing a contract. Allow two to three weeks for agencies to write proposals, one to two weeks for presentations and reference calls, and time for legal review and contracts. Rushing the proposal window usually leads to less thoughtful responses.

Method

## The math, stated plainly

Every NativeCode product publishes its assumptions on the page. This is the sequence the engine follows.

1. 01

    ### Measure the band

    `band = underbust, snug, rounded to nearest even`

    The snug ribcage measurement is the band. The modern method does not add four inches. That rule dates from stiffer fabrics and is the most common source of wrong sizes.

2. 02

    ### Measure the bust

    `cup = bust − band · 1″ per cup`

    A loose measurement across the fullest point. One inch of difference is an A, two is a B, three a C, four a D, then DD and beyond.

3. 03

    ### Convert across regions

    `US 34C → EU 75C → FR 90C → AU 12C`

    Band numbers change by system (inches, centimetres, or dress-size-style numbers), and cup ladders diverge above D. The converter handles both.

4. 04

    ### Offer sister sizes

    `32D ≈ 34C ≈ 36B`

    Cup volume is relative to band. Going down a band and up a cup keeps the volume the same, which is how a shopper fixes a brand that runs tight.

FAQ

## Questions about Brasize.ai

What do I need to use the calculator?

Two measurements: a snug underbust, taken level around the ribcage directly under the bust, and a loose bust measurement across the fullest point with the tape resting, not pulled. Inches or centimetres both work. The calculator turns the underbust into the band and the bust-band difference into the cup.

Which sizing systems does it return?

Brasize.ai returns US, UK, EU, AU and FR sizes, each with band, cup, full size and sister sizes. Showing the same size in every system a shopper will meet means an online order from a foreign brand lands right. The converter also handles cup ladders that diverge above D.

What is a sister size?

A sister size has the same cup volume on a different band. A 34C, 32D and 36B hold roughly the same volume, so going down a band and up a cup keeps the volume the same. Shoppers use sister sizes when a band runs tight or loose in a particular brand.

Why doesn't it add four inches to the band?

Because that rule dates from an era of non-stretch fabrics and produces bands that are too loose. Brasize.ai uses the modern snug-measure method, where the snug ribcage measurement is the band. The site explains the old rule and retires it, since it is the most common source of wrong sizes.

Is it free?

Yes. Brasize.ai is free to use with no sign-up. Visitors can run the calculator and browse the sizing reference, which runs to more than 700 pages covering sizes by region, cup-size charts, breast shapes, bra styles and brand-by-brand comparisons, without creating an account.

Method

## The math, stated plainly

Every NativeCode product publishes its assumptions on the page. This is the sequence the engine follows.

1. 01

    ### From the last period

    `EDD = LMP + 280 days`

    The standard convention. It assumes a 28-day cycle with ovulation near day 14; a different cycle length shifts the estimate by the difference from 28.

2. 02

    ### From conception

    `EDD = conception + 266 days`

    Two weeks fewer than the LMP count, which is why 40 weeks from the last period is roughly 38 weeks of development.

3. 03

    ### From IVF transfer

    `EDD = transfer + 266 − embryo age`

    A day-5 blastocyst is transfer + 261 days. Because the embryo's age is known exactly, this is the most precise self-calculation available.

4. 04

    ### Confirmed by ultrasound

    A first-trimester crown-rump measurement is the most accurate dating method. When it disagrees significantly with LMP dating, clinicians rely on the ultrasound, and only a clinician sets the official date.

    ### Project the next period

    `next period = last period + cycle length`

    A cycle is counted from the first day of bleeding to the day before the next bleed. The site projects three cycles, not one.

2. 02

    ### Count back to ovulation

    `ovulation = next period − luteal phase`

    The luteal phase holds near 14 days for most people while the follicular phase absorbs the variation, so counting backward is more reliable than the day-14 rule.

3. 03

    ### Bracket the fertile window

    `window = 5 days before ovulation + ovulation day`

    Sperm survive up to five days; the egg about one. Conception is likeliest in the final two days.

4. 04

    ### Calibrate to real data

    In an analysis of more than 600,000 cycles, only a minority were exactly 28 days. Entering real averages instead of defaults is what narrows the window.

The next three periods and today's phase, without an account or a tracking pixel.

### People trying to conceive

A fertile window that moves with cycle length instead of assuming day 14.

FAQ

## Questions about PeriodCalculator.ai

How does it estimate ovulation?

By subtracting the luteal phase, 14 days by default and adjustable, from the projected next period. The luteal phase is far steadier than the cycle itself, so counting back is more reliable than the day-14 rule. On a 35-day cycle, estimated ovulation lands around day 21, not day 14.

Can it be used to avoid pregnancy?

No. The site is explicit that a calendar calculator is an awareness tool, not contraception, and its avoid-pregnancy mode shows estimated risk only. Ranges are shown as ranges, estimates are labelled as estimates, and the page lists clinical thresholds that are reasons to see a clinician.

Is anything I enter saved?

No. Every calculation runs in the browser, and nothing is transmitted, stored or tracked. PeriodCalculator.ai is private by architecture, so it shows the next three periods and the current cycle phase without an account or a tracking pixel. Your dates stay on your device.

How accurate is it?

With regular cycles, predictions are typically within a day or two. With irregular cycles, the site tells you to read each date as the center of a window. Entering your real average cycle and period length instead of the defaults is what narrows the window, since few cycles are exactly 28 days.

Is it medically reviewed?

Review by a board-certified OB-GYN is in progress, and the page says so. The reviewer byline publishes at launch. In the meantime the methodology cites ACOG patient guidance and large-scale cycle datasets published in peer-reviewed journals, and the content is written to clinical-review standards.

# TDEE.co TDEE, BMR and Macro Calculator

Source: https://www.nativecode.ai/products/tdee (updated 2026-11-16)

Overview

## What TDEE.co is

TDEE.co answers the question behind every diet and training plan: how many calories do I actually burn in a day? It estimates basal metabolic rate with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, switches to Katch-McArdle when a body-fat percentage is supplied, and multiplies by an honest activity factor between 1.2 and 1.9.

Every number the site produces lives on the same axis (resting burn, activity energy, the maintenance line, a goal deficit or surplus, and a macro split), so a visitor can see how one result becomes the next rather than juggling seven unrelated calculators.

The page is medically reviewed, cites its equations, and is structured for answer engines: fifteen definition-first FAQs written to be quoted, a formula shown in full, and an accuracy section that says plainly what a calculator cannot see.

Method

## The math, stated plainly

Every NativeCode product publishes its assumptions on the page. This is the sequence the engine follows.

1. 01

    ### Estimate resting burn

    `BMR = 10·kg + 6.25·cm − 5·age + 5 (men) / − 161 (women)`

    Mifflin-St Jeor is the default, recognised by the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics as the most accurate general-population equation.

2. 02

    ### Scale by activity

    `TDEE = BMR × 1.2 … 1.9`

    The multiplier is the single biggest variable. The site tells people to match an average week, not a best one. A desk job plus four hard sessions is ×1.55.

3. 03

    ### Refine with body fat

    `BMR = 370 + 21.6 × lean mass (kg)`

    Entering a body-fat percentage switches the engine to Katch-McArdle, which is driven by lean mass rather than total weight.

4. 04

    ### Steer to a goal

    `−500 → ~1 lb/wk · +250 → lean gain`

    Deficits and surpluses are applied to the maintenance line, with a low-calorie warning threshold of about 1,200 (women) and 1,500 (men).

Reviewed by a board-certified family-medicine physician, with a named reviewer page and a last-reviewed date on the page itself.

Built on the peer-reviewed Mifflin-St Jeor (1990), Katch-McArdle, and revised Harris-Benedict (1984) equations.

FAQ

## Questions about TDEE.co

What does TDEE.co calculate?

It calculates total daily energy expenditure, the calories you burn in a day, plus your BMR, calorie targets for losing, maintaining or gaining weight, and a suggested macro split. Every number sits on the same energy axis, so you can see how one result becomes the next.

Which formula does it use?

Mifflin-St Jeor by default, which the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics recognises as the most accurate general-population equation. If you enter a body-fat percentage, it switches to Katch-McArdle, which uses lean body mass. The result is then multiplied by an activity factor between 1.2 and 1.9.

Is it free?

Yes. Every calculator on tdee.co is free, with no account, sign-up or ads. That covers the TDEE, BMR, macro, calorie deficit, maintenance calorie, calorie, body fat and protein calculators, which all share one logic layer, so their answers never disagree with each other.

How accurate is the result?

Typically within 5 to 10 percent of true daily burn. No formula can see genetics, hormones, sleep, stress or everyday movement, so the site recommends holding the target for two to three weeks, then adjusting by 100 to 200 calories against your weight trend.

Who reviews the content?

A board-certified family-medicine physician reviews the content. The reviewer, their credentials and the last-reviewed date are published on the page. The calculators are built on the peer-reviewed Mifflin-St Jeor, Katch-McArdle and revised Harris-Benedict equations, and the page cites each one.

Method

## The math, stated plainly

Every NativeCode product publishes its assumptions on the page. This is the sequence the engine follows.

1. 01

    ### Normalise to seconds

    `t = h·3600 + m·60 + s`

    Every clock time is converted to total seconds, the change is applied, and the result is normalised back to a 12- or 24-hour clock, tracking day rollover.

2. 02

    ### Measure across midnight

    `if end < start: end += 24h`

    When an end time is earlier than the start, the calculator can treat it as the next day, so 11:00 PM to 2:30 AM reads 3h 30m.

3. 03

    ### Convert to payroll hours

    `paid = out − in − break · decimal = minutes ÷ 60`

    Thirty minutes is 0.5 hours, forty-five is 0.75. Every work-hour result shows both clock and decimal formats.

4. 04

    ### Walk the calendar

    Date math applies month lengths and leap years correctly rather than assuming 30-day months, and reports the day of week for the result.

FAQ

## Decatur SEO company questions

### Do you work with small businesses in Decatur?

Yes. NativeCode is Atlanta-based, with its office in Norcross, and scopes local work to the size of the business, from a single storefront to several locations. Small businesses usually start with the Google Business Profile, reviews and one strong page before anything else is added.

### How can a local restaurant or shop beat chains in Google Maps?

Chains often have generic profiles. A local business with accurate categories, real photos, current hours, a menu or product list and frequent reviews can outrank them nearby. Replying to reviews and posting updates also shows Google and customers that the business is active.

### Should my site say Decatur or Atlanta?

Use Decatur if that is your address. Many people search Decatur by name, and Google uses your verified address for map results either way. If you also serve Atlanta neighborhoods, add pages for them rather than replacing Decatur, so you stay relevant for both.

### How many reviews do we need?

There is no fixed number. A steady flow of recent, detailed reviews matters more than a single burst, and responding to each one helps. We set up a simple way to ask customers after a visit or purchase, so reviews keep coming without extra work from your team.

FAQ

## Duluth SEO company questions

### Do you work with businesses in Duluth and Gwinnett?

Yes. NativeCode is Atlanta-based, with its office in Norcross, next door to Duluth, and works with Duluth and Gwinnett businesses in person or remotely. Programs are scoped to the business, from a single storefront to several locations across the county.

### How should a bilingual site be set up for SEO?

Give each language its own URL, link the versions with hreflang tags and translate titles, descriptions and page content fully rather than mixing languages on one page. We build the structure, and translation is done by your team or a translator you trust.

### Does Google Business Profile support more than one language?

The profile has one primary language, but your description, posts and photos can reach both audiences, and reviews in either language count. Keeping your name, address and phone number the same everywhere matters more than the language of each individual listing.

### Can we rank in Suwanee or Lawrenceville from Duluth?

In regular search, yes, with a useful page for each area. Map results favor businesses close to the searcher, so service area businesses should list those cities as service areas. Each area page needs real local detail to rank, not a copy with the city name changed.

FAQ

## Local SEO questions

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Alabama?

Yes. NativeCode is an Atlanta-based agency that works remotely with businesses across Alabama. We plan over video calls, work directly in your Google Business Profile and site, and use your own photos and job details so your listings show real Alabama work. We do not have an office in Alabama.

### Can one business rank in both Birmingham and Huntsville?

Google Maps favors businesses close to the searcher, so one address rarely shows in both. If you have a real location in each city, each needs its own Business Profile and location page. Check Apple Maps, Bing Places and Yelp at least once a year so old or mismatched details do not linger.

### How should a Gulf Coast business plan for seasonal searches?

Update hours, photos and posts before the busy season starts in Gulf Shores and Orange Beach. Answer common visitor questions on your site, such as parking, booking and pet rules. AI tools often pull from answers like these. Writing your service details as short, direct answers makes it easier for AI tools to quote you accurately.

### Do reviews matter as much in small Alabama towns?

Yes. A small town may have only a few competitors, so a steady flow of recent reviews can set you apart. Ask happy customers, reply to every review and keep your profile details current. Never offer a discount or gift for a review, since Google prohibits incentivized reviews and can remove them.

Alaska search follows the road system and the seasons. Anchorage, Fairbanks and Juneau are the main hubs, with the Mat-Su Valley and Kenai Peninsula close behind. Juneau and much of Southeast Alaska can only be reached by air or water.

01

### Summer visitor season

Cruise passengers and summer visitors arrive in Juneau, Ketchikan, Skagway and Seward. Tour operators and shops need listings and pages ready before the season starts.

02

### Rural and bush service areas

Many villages are reached only by plane or boat. Contractors and suppliers serving them should describe service areas clearly instead of relying on one map pin.

03

### Winter hours and conditions

Long dark winters change when people shop and travel. Keep winter hours, holiday closures and road access notes current so Google and AI tools show accurate details.

FAQ

## Local SEO questions

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Alaska?

Yes. NativeCode is an Atlanta-based agency that works remotely with businesses across Alaska. We plan over video calls, work directly in your Google Business Profile and site, and use your own photos and job details so your listings show real Alaska work. We do not have an office in Alaska.

### How do I reach customers in towns far from my location?

Maps results stay close to the searcher, so distant towns are hard to reach through Maps alone. Build a page for each region you serve, such as the Kenai Peninsula or Mat-Su Valley, and explain how you get there. Each area page should name real projects, streets or landmarks there, since near-duplicate pages that only swap the city name rarely rank.

### Should tour businesses change their profiles for summer?

Yes. Update hours, booking links, photos and posts before the summer season. Add answers to common questions about departures, weather and what to bring. AI tools often draw on that detail when travelers plan. Plain answers to common customer questions on your own site give Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT clear text to quote.

### Does a service-area business need a public address?

No. If customers do not visit your location, you can hide the address and list the areas you serve instead. This is common for plumbers, electricians and other trades working across Anchorage and the Valley. Review your listings on Apple Maps, Bing Places and the main local directories once a year and fix any old details.

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Albuquerque?

FAQ

## Local SEO questions

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Anchorage?

Yes. NativeCode is an Atlanta-based agency that works remotely with Anchorage businesses. We plan over video calls, work directly in your Google Business Profile and site, and use your own photos and job details so your listings show real Anchorage work. We do not have an Anchorage office.

### Can I rank in Wasilla and Palmer from Anchorage?

Partly. Maps results favor nearby businesses, so an Anchorage address will show less often for searches in the Valley. A clear service area and a Mat-Su page on your site can help you appear in organic results there. Review your listings on Apple Maps, Bing Places and the main local directories once a year and fix any old details.

### How do I handle winter hours in Google?

Set regular hours for winter and use special hours for holidays and weather closures. Post updates when conditions change. Accurate hours reduce wasted trips and frustrated reviews. Never offer a discount or gift for a review, since Google prohibits incentivized reviews and can remove them.

### Is it worth targeting summer visitors and locals separately?

Often, yes. Visitors search for tours, rentals and things to do near downtown. Locals search for services near home. Separate pages and posts let you speak to each group without mixing messages. Set special hours in your Google Business Profile ahead of time so Maps and AI answers do not show outdated hours on busy days.

## Local SEO questions

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Arkansas?

Yes. NativeCode is an Atlanta-based agency that works remotely with businesses across Arkansas. We plan over video calls, work directly in your Google Business Profile and site, and use your own photos and job details so your listings show real Arkansas work. We do not have an office in Arkansas.

### Can one profile cover all of Northwest Arkansas?

One profile can show in nearby searches, but Maps favors distance. If you serve Bentonville through Fayetteville, list each city in your service areas and build pages that show real work in each one. Each area page should name real projects, streets or landmarks there, since near-duplicate pages that only swap the city name rarely rank.

### How do I handle customers from both Arkansas and Texas?

Name both sides in your service areas if you serve them. Create pages for each side of Texarkana, and list any licenses that apply in each state. Clear details help Google and customers understand your reach. Local rankings depend on distance, relevance and prominence, so a complete profile, accurate categories and recent reviews all count.

### Do rural Arkansas customers use Google Maps?

Yes. People in rural Arkansas still search on their phones for repairs, food and services. They may drive farther, so complete hours, phone numbers and directions on your profile matter a lot. Choosing the most accurate primary category in your Google Business Profile is one of the simplest ways to match more searches.

## Local SEO questions

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Birmingham?

Yes. NativeCode is an Atlanta-based agency that works remotely with Birmingham businesses. We plan over video calls, work directly in your Google Business Profile and site, and use your own photos and job details so your listings show real Birmingham work. We do not have a Birmingham office.

### Should I target Birmingham or the suburb where my office is?

Target both, but be honest about your address. Your Business Profile should show your real location. Service pages for places like Hoover or Homewood can explain how you serve them without claiming an office there. Check Apple Maps, Bing Places and Yelp at least once a year so old or mismatched details do not linger.

### Does being in Shelby County hurt my Birmingham visibility?

Not by itself. Google weighs distance from the searcher, so a Pelham or Chelsea business may show for nearby searches but less for downtown ones. Strong reviews and a complete profile help at the edges of that range. Never offer a discount or gift for a review, since Google prohibits incentivized reviews and can remove them.

### What should a medical practice near UAB do first?

Verify your Business Profile, pick the most accurate primary category and list each provider correctly. Add parking and entrance details, since the Southside can be confusing for new patients. Then add schema to your location page. Each area page should name real projects, streets or landmarks there, since near-duplicate pages that only swap the city name rarely rank.

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Burlington?

Yes. NativeCode is an Atlanta-based agency that works remotely with Burlington businesses. We plan over video calls, work directly in your Google Business Profile and site, and use your own photos and job details so your listings show real Burlington work. We do not have a Burlington office.

### Can a Burlington business rank in Williston or Essex?

Partly. Map results lean toward the closest options, so a downtown Burlington address has less pull in Williston or Essex. A service area, useful town pages and reviews from customers there can help organic visibility. Map placement is not guaranteed.

### Should Burlington businesses publish French content for Quebec visitors?

If French-speaking visitors are a real share of your customers, a French page for key services or menus can help. Keep your business name, address and phone number identical in every language version so search engines treat them as one business.

### How do winter and summer change Burlington search?

Summer brings lake, waterfront and patio searches, while winter shifts attention to ski trips and indoor spots. Update hours, photos and Business Profile posts as each season starts so listings match what you offer. Check Apple Maps, Bing Places and Yelp at least once a year so old or mismatched details do not linger.

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in California?

We plan over video calls, work directly in your Google Business Profile and site, and use your own photos and job details so your listings show real California work. ### Should a Southern California business target the Bay Area too?

### Can a business rank in many California cities at once?

## Local SEO questions

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Charlotte?

Yes. NativeCode is an Atlanta-based agency that works remotely with Charlotte businesses. We plan over video calls, work directly in your Google Business Profile and site, and use your own photos and job details so your listings show real Charlotte work. We do not have a Charlotte office.

### Should my Charlotte business target Fort Mill and Rock Hill?

If you serve customers there, it can help. Add those cities to your service areas and build a page about your work in York County. Google weighs distance, so map rankings across the state line may stay harder. Write each area page around real work you have done there; pages that only swap the town name rarely help.

### How many locations should be on my Google Business Profile?

Use one profile per real, staffed location. If you have offices in Ballantyne and University City, each can have its own profile. Profiles for addresses without staff or signage break Google's rules and can be suspended. Check Apple Maps, Bing Places and Yelp at least once a year so old or mismatched details do not linger.

### Does schema markup help Charlotte businesses in AI answers?

Schema tells search engines your business type, address, hours and services in a structured way. It does not guarantee AI mentions, but it makes your details easier to read and match. We add LocalBusiness schema to each location page. Plain answers to common customer questions on your own site give Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT clear text to quote.

## Local SEO questions

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Colorado?

Yes. NativeCode is an Atlanta-based agency that works remotely with businesses across Colorado. We plan over video calls, work directly in your Google Business Profile and site, and use your own photos and job details so your listings show real Colorado work. We do not have an office in Colorado.

### How should a mountain town business plan for ski season?

Update hours, photos and posts before the season opens. Add answers about parking, shuttles and rentals. Check your profile again before summer, when demand often shifts to hiking and biking. A useful area page describes real jobs, travel times or customers in that place rather than repeating the same text.

### Can I serve Denver and Boulder from one location?

You can serve both, but Maps will favor your real address. Build a page for the city you are not in, with real details about your work there, and list both in your service areas. Check Apple Maps, Bing Places and Yelp at least once a year so old or mismatched details do not linger.

### Do Western Slope towns need a different approach?

Often, yes. Grand Junction and nearby towns have fewer competitors and longer drives. Clear service areas, complete hours and strong reviews help when customers come from far away. Google prohibits offering discounts or gifts for reviews, so the safest approach is to ask every customer soon after the job.

### Fairfield County and New York

Stamford, Greenwich and Norwalk sit within reach of New York City. Businesses there compete with New York firms in some searches and should state their local address clearly.

02

### Shoreline summer season

Mystic, Old Saybrook and other shoreline towns get busier in summer. Restaurants, marinas and inns need seasonal hours and current photos ready before visitors arrive.

03

### College towns

Yale in New Haven and UConn in Storrs bring students and visiting families each term. Restaurants, hotels and movers see demand tied to move in and graduation weeks.

FAQ

## Local SEO questions

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Connecticut?

Yes. NativeCode is an Atlanta-based agency that works remotely with businesses across Connecticut. We plan over video calls, work directly in your Google Business Profile and site, and use your own photos and job details so your listings show real Connecticut work. We do not have an office in Connecticut.

### Should I build a page for each Connecticut town I serve?

Only for towns where you do real work and have something specific to say. Connecticut towns are small and close together, so pick the ones that matter most and write useful pages for each. Google weighs distance, relevance and prominence for local results, so a complete profile and steady reviews still matter.

### Can a Stamford business compete with New York firms?

In map results, your nearby address helps for local searches. Show Connecticut details on your pages, such as the towns you serve and any state licenses. That helps customers who want someone close by. Review your listings on Apple Maps, Bing Places and the main local directories once a year and fix any old details.

### How do I prepare for summer on the shoreline?

Update hours, add seasonal photos and post about events or reservations before summer. Answer common questions about parking and booking on your site. AI tools often draw on those answers. Writing your service details as short, direct answers makes it easier for AI tools to quote you accurately.

FAQ

## Local SEO questions

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Dallas?

Yes. NativeCode is an Atlanta-based agency that works remotely with Dallas businesses. We run audits and planning over video calls, get access to your Google Business Profile and site, and use your real photos and job details so your listings reflect actual Dallas work. We do not have a Dallas office.

### How do I rank in Google Maps in Dallas?

Start with a complete Google Business Profile at your real address, the right primary category and steady, recent reviews. Then build a page on your site for each service and for the Dallas areas you really serve. Maps favors businesses close to the searcher, so placement varies across the metro and is never guaranteed.

### Can a Dallas business rank in Plano and Frisco too?

In organic results, yes, if you build useful pages for Plano and Frisco with real projects and details. In Google Maps, distance matters, so a Dallas address has limited reach in Collin County. If you have a staffed location there, give it its own profile and page.

### Do Dallas businesses need Spanish SEO?

Many do. Dallas has a large Spanish-speaking population, so service pages written by a fluent speaker can reach customers who search in Spanish. List Spanish as a language on your profile, tag the pages with hreflang and answer Spanish reviews in Spanish.

## Local SEO questions

### Does NativeCode work with businesses in Denver?

01

### East Village and Court Avenue

Shops, bars and restaurants cluster in the East Village and along Court Avenue. Clear categories, hours and photos help nearby searchers pick you.

02

### State Fair season

The Iowa State Fair brings visitors to the east side each August. Nearby restaurants, hotels and services benefit from event posts and updated hours.

03

### Insurance and office clusters

Des Moines has a large insurance and financial services sector. B2B firms serving those offices need search terms and pages built for professional buyers.
